questions.question: What is the very first thing you should do locally before starting work on a new feature branch in a team repository?

options.B: Switch to `main` and run `git pull` to ensure your base is 100% up to date with teammates' work

questions.explanation: Always branch off a fresh, updated `main` to avoid starting work from stale code.

questions.question: Why should developers NEVER push unfinished, broken code directly to `main`?

options.A: `main` represents the stable, working version of the application; breaking it blocks all teammates and halts production deployments
options.B: Git automatically deletes repositories that contain bugs
options.C: GitHub charges a fee for broken commits
options.D: It is physically impossible to push to main

questions.explanation: Protecting `main` ensures the team always has a releasable, functional foundation.

questions.question: Which sequence accurately summarizes the full end-to-end collaborative developer workflow?

options.A: Issue → Feature Branch → Commit → Push → Pull Request → Code Review → Merge → Pull to Local
options.B: Commit to Main → PR → Branch → Issue

questions.explanation: This 8-step cycle is the gold standard industry workflow used worldwide.

questions.question: What does the command `git status` tell you?

options.B: Your active branch, tracked/untracked files, staged changes, and whether your local branch is ahead/behind remote

questions.explanation: `git status` is your constant situational awareness tool in Git.

questions.question: What is an 'atomic commit'?

options.A: A commit that uses nuclear physics
options.B: A small, self-contained commit that solves one single logical task or bug cleanly and completely

questions.explanation: Atomic commits are easy to understand, easy to review, and easy to revert if a bug is introduced.

questions.question: If a commit introduced a critical bug in production, which command is the safest way to undo it on a public branch?
questions.explanation: `git revert` records a new commit that safely reverses the bug without rewriting public branch history.

questions.question: How can you check who wrote each line of a file and when it was committed?
questions.explanation: `git blame` annotates each line of a file with the commit hash, author name, and date of the last edit.

questions.question: What is `git stash` used for?

options.A: To temporarily shelve uncommitted changes so you can switch branches or pull without committing incomplete work

questions.explanation: `git stash` temporarily stores modified files in a clean scratchpad, allowing you to restore them later with `git stash pop`.

questions.question: Which of the following belongs in a professional GitHub repository before sharing with employers or mentors?

options.A: Committed `.env` files with secret API keys
options.B: A clear README.md, a proper .gitignore, descriptive commit messages, and a clean branch history

questions.explanation: Repository hygiene demonstrates professional engineering habits and attention to detail.

questions.question: Having completed this 15-day Git & GitHub programme, what should be your standard practice for all future coding projects?

options.A: Go back to saving folders as `project_v2_final.zip`
options.B: Initialize Git (`git init`), create a `.gitignore` and `README.md`, work on feature branches, and push to GitHub regularly
options.C: Only use Git the night before project submission

questions.explanation: Making Git a daily reflex protects your work, empowers teamwork, and sets you apart as a professional engineer.
